analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote and died in committee, despite 110 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Weeks after Congress passed the 2003 Medicare drug benefit, which barred the government from negotiating drug prices, this bill would have removed that ban. It directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate with drug makers for the lowest possible prices, the same way the VA and other federal buyers do. Medicare pays for tens of millions of seniors' prescriptions, so negotiated prices would have lowered drug costs for beneficiaries and reduced taxpayer spending. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare, who would pay less for prescriptions through Part D plans; taxpayers, who fund the Medicare drug benefit and would pay less per prescription; the federal government, which would gain purchasing power it lacks under the 2003 law's 'non-interference' clause.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the 'non-interference' provision the 2003 Medicare drug law added, which prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering with negotiations between drug makers and private Part D plans [S3].

It instead requires the Secretary to negotiate contracts with manufacturers of covered Part D drugs, with authority similar to other federal agencies that buy drugs in bulk, 'to ensure that beneficiaries... pay the lowest possible price' [S3].
The CRS summary describes the same purpose: giving the Secretary authority to negotiate prices to contain costs while providing quality care [S2].

Medicare is one of the largest drug buyers in the world; bulk purchasers like the VA historically pay far less per prescription than Medicare beneficiaries do under the plan structure the 2003 law created.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenue per prescription sold through Medicare would fall under negotiated prices. Private Part D plans and the drug middlemen they use would also face a changed role if the government negotiated directly.

drawbacks.text: Pharmaceutical makers argued that government price negotiation would reduce their revenue and could slow the development of new medicines; the bill's negotiator would hold enormous leverage over an industry that depends on high U.S. prices to fund research [S3].

The bill gave the Secretary broad, undefined negotiating authority ('authority similar to that of other Federal entities') without specifying negotiation methods, formulary rules, or savings targets, leaving how it would work in practice to future administrative decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is direct: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers would pay less for prescriptions because the largest public drug buyer would gain the negotiating power other federal buyers already have. The main cost falls on drug manufacturers, and the strongest honest concern is that lower prices could mean less industry revenue available for research into new drugs, though the bill leaves the strength of that tradeoff to how negotiations are actually conducted. The bill is simple and targeted rather than badly designed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, sat there with no hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 8, 2003, less than a month after the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act was signed into law [S1].
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On December 17, 2003, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; no further action was recorded [S5].
It had 110 cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to sponsor Rep. Chet Edwards [S4].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the 2003 law's ban on Medicare price negotiation stayed in place, and private insurers and drug intermediaries kept their role as the channel through which Medicare pays for prescriptions. Beneficiaries and taxpayers continued to pay the higher, un-negotiated prices.

for.name: 110 of 205 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi and the ranking members of the health and tax committees

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or markup; it went to the Health subcommittee on December 17, 2003, and stayed there

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on referral and never took it up

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the non-interference ban the bill would have repealed; the industry had just secured that ban in the 2003 Medicare law and opposed giving the government negotiating authority

sides.party_line_note: All 111 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled House committees never gave it a hearing [S4].

industries.note: Medicare negotiation would directly cut the prices manufacturers receive on prescriptions for tens of millions of seniors. Their interest in keeping negotiation off the table ran against beneficiaries and taxpayers, who pay the difference.

industries.industry: Private Part D prescription drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The 2003 law made private plans the exclusive channel for Medicare drug coverage and barred government negotiation, guaranteeing them that role. This bill would have begun shifting pricing power back to the government, thinning their margin on Medicare drug dollars.
